problem: "Both are set once and then follow the app for its whole life" is false for the version numbers. versionCode must be increased on every single upload; only the signing key is set once. A student who remembers the lead will reuse versionCode and get rejected uploads.
fix: Say that the signing key is created once and kept for the app's life, while versionCode must rise on every upload and versionName is updated to label each release.

where: Exam traps, fifth trap ("Testing only the debug build")
problem: The claim that "certificate-restricted API keys fail only in release" is inverted. An API key restricted to the release certificate (package name plus release SHA-1, the usual Maps setup) fails in the debug build, because the debug APK is signed with the per-machine debug key. Registering the release fingerprint in the console is what makes the key work in release. The same confusion appears in Section 3, where the reader is told to test screens that call "a key restricted to the release certificate".
fix: Keep shrinking (R8 renaming or deleting reflectively used classes) as the release-only failure. Say that a key restricted to one certificate works only in builds signed with that certificate: keys registered with the debug SHA-1 fail in release, and keys registered with the release SHA-1 fail in debug, so register both fingerprints and test both builds.

problem: The question asks for two ways out, but the answer gives one: upload with a code greater than 12. There is no second, distinct remedy.
fix: Either ask for one way out, or give two: bump to 13 (or higher), and, if the clash came from an old draft release, remove or halt that draft before re-uploading with the higher code.

problem: The node "Sign with keystore" is placed before "Build release APK". In a Gradle release build the signing step runs at the end, after compiling, shrinking and packaging, so the diagram shows the steps in the wrong order.
fix: Order the nodes as: set versionCode, build release APK (shrink and minify), sign with the release keystore, test the signed APK, deploy. The caption stays true: testing follows signing.

problem: "It proves who built it" overstates what a self-signed certificate does. There is no certificate authority behind an Android signing key, so the signature proves the APK comes from whoever holds that key, not a verified identity.
fix: Write that the signature ties the APK to the holder of the private key, which is how Android recognises an update to the same app.
